claims.text: Slower movement can make washing and dressing take longer. Balance and gait changes increase fall risk.
Physical and occupational therapy can support walking and daily function. Exercise may improve balance, flexibility and strength; a clinician should review new exercise plans.
A quiet voice, rapid speech or hesitation can make communication difficult. Speech therapy can support communication.
Chewing and swallowing problems may cause choking, drooling or reduced intake. Speech and swallowing support may be needed.
Depression, anxiety, constipation and urinary symptoms are also part of Parkinson disease; care extends beyond tremor.
Blood pressure can fall on standing, causing lightheadedness or fainting. Sleep disruption and daytime sleepiness may also affect daily safety.
Fiber and fluids may help constipation when consistent with the person’s nutrition and fluid plan.
Dietary protein can affect carbidopa-levodopa absorption. Review food and medicine timing with the treating team; this guide gives no protein-restriction regimen.
Speech therapy can help preserve communication as speech becomes less clear.
Speech-generating devices may use eye tracking. Voice banking records the person’s own voice for possible later use.
Physical therapy can support movement, reduce falls and joint discomfort, and maintain independence. Rehabilitation should match individual needs.
Occupational therapy can identify feeding, bathing and grooming aids that make self-care easier.
Dietitians can plan small, nutritious meals when chewing or swallowing becomes difficult. Feeding support requires individualized planning.
Breathing-muscle weakness may cause breathlessness during activity, at night or when lying down. Noninvasive ventilation can provide breathing support.
A weakened cough may need assistance to clear secretions. Respiratory support options include prescribed cough-assist devices.
Increasing dependence can place substantial demands on caregivers. Home-care services and caregiver support can help sustain care.
Guillain-Barré syndrome can affect breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Hospital monitoring helps identify complications as weakness changes.
Swallowing weakness can cause choking and pneumonia; swallowing support remains relevant during recovery.
Physical rehabilitation helps restore strength and daily function after acute stabilization.
Therapists may use positioning and limb movement to preserve flexibility. Exercises can target weaker muscles when stronger muscles compensate for them.
Occupational therapy can help a person find new ways to manage everyday activities.
Vocational therapy and adaptive equipment may help with work demands and persistent functional limitations.
Recovery varies and may take weeks to years. Some people continue to have weakness, numbness, fatigue or pain.
Sudden dependence can be emotionally difficult. Counseling and peer support can help people adjust; recovery is not only a strength goal.

entries.title: Peripheral neuropathy: daily function and safety

claims.text: Sensory neuropathy can reduce awareness of pain, temperature and limb position. Motor involvement may cause weakness or cramps.
Autonomic involvement can affect sweating, blood pressure and digestion; neuropathy does not always present as painful feet.
Loss of position sense can affect balance, walking and tasks such as fastening buttons.
Appropriate braces or orthopedic footwear can support walking and help prevent foot injuries when motor nerves are affected.
Nerve pain may worsen at night or occur with light touch, including contact with bedsheets.
Counseling and other behavioral approaches may help with chronic pain and associated anxiety or depression.
Evaluation includes medical conditions, medicines, alcohol or toxin exposure, and vitamin deficiencies. Treatment depends on the cause and nerve pattern.
Managing diabetes and other contributing conditions may improve symptoms. Discuss medication changes with the clinician; do not stop treatment independently.

entries.title: Cirrhosis: nutrition and daily food planning

claims.text: Cirrhosis can impair digestion and nutrient absorption. Nausea or vomiting may further reduce food intake.
Dietitian support can help match calories, protein and other nutrients to disease severity and individual needs.
Cirrhosis changes how the body stores and uses energy. Long periods without food can be a concern.
The care team may recommend smaller, frequent meals and a bedtime snack or early breakfast.
Sodium limits may be recommended. Use the person’s prescribed plan instead of applying one limit to everyone.
Review vitamins, herbs and other supplements with the clinician; supplementation depends on identified needs.
Raw or undercooked seafood and meat, and unpasteurized dairy products, can cause severe infections in people with cirrhosis.
Alcohol can cause additional liver damage. NIDDK advises complete avoidance of alcohol in cirrhosis.
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency can cause loose, greasy, foul-smelling stools, bloating, abdominal discomfort and weight loss.
It can occur with pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer or pancreatic and upper gastrointestinal surgery.
Prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy helps digest food and improve nutrient absorption.
NIDDK describes taking prescribed enzymes during meals and snacks. Follow the individual product and clinician instructions; this guide does not set doses.
A dietitian may recommend smaller, more frequent meals and other changes based on the underlying condition.
Alcohol avoidance and smoking cessation may be part of treatment. Food changes should address nutritional needs as well as symptoms.
Follow-up may assess malnutrition, low levels of vitamins A, D, E and K, and reduced bone mass.
Vitamin or other nutrient supplements may be recommended for identified deficits. Discuss supplements with the clinician before starting them.
Severe infection or diarrhea, or vomiting that prevents retention of corticosteroid tablets, requires immediate medical attention. These situations can lead to adrenal crisis.
Illness, injury and surgery can change steroid requirements. The clinician supplies the individual adjustment plan; this guide does not provide a dose multiplier.
Sudden severe back, abdominal or leg pain, vomiting, diarrhea, marked weakness, confusion or loss of consciousness may signal adrenal crisis. Emergency assessment is needed.
Adrenal crisis can be life-threatening. Emergency medication preparation complements urgent medical care; it does not replace assessment.
Medical-alert identification or an emergency card can communicate adrenal insufficiency when the person cannot explain it.
NIDDK advises carrying prescribed emergency corticosteroid injection supplies and ensuring family or friends know when and how to use them.
Surgery under general anesthesia may require intravenous hormone replacement until oral treatment is possible. Discuss the plan with the treating team before surgery.
The clinician adjusts treatment back toward the usual regimen as illness or injury resolves. Recovery instructions are part of the plan.
Fatigue, cold intolerance and weight changes can occur with hypothyroidism, but symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.
Blood tests and clinical assessment help evaluate thyroid function and the cause of symptoms.
Thyroid hormone replacement controls hypothyroidism when taken as prescribed. Do not stop it without discussing the plan with the clinician.
Excess thyroid replacement can cause harm, including atrial fibrillation or bone loss; symptom changes do not justify unsupervised dose changes.
Blood testing follows treatment initiation and dose changes. The clinician uses results to adjust therapy and arrange ongoing checks.
Notify the clinician promptly if pregnancy occurs because thyroid replacement needs may change.
Excess iodine, including iodine supplements or large amounts of seaweed, can worsen some autoimmune thyroid disorders.
Discuss supplements and iodine-containing cough medicines with the care team. Pregnancy-related iodine needs require individualized advice.
